slide.title: Design, Then Build
slide.body: Left: a one-page design sheet with six labelled sections. Right: a connected workflow with a trigger, a switch and an agent node. Small tag: AI Agents and Automation Workflows · Lesson 15 · Capstone.

scenes.voiceover: You now have every part: triggers, Sheets, the Claude API, validation, routing, tools, memory, approval and error handling. In the capstone, you put them together to automate one real business process, from the first input to the final action.

slide.title: Two capstone steps
slide.body: Step 1 (this lesson): design + first working version. Step 2 (Lesson 16): test, harden, present.

scenes.voiceover: The capstone has two steps. In this lesson, you design and build a first working version. In the next lesson, you test it, make it reliable, and present it.

slide.title: Choose a process
slide.body: Real, repeated, clear inputs and outputs. Examples: supplier invoice intake · event registration · customer enquiry triage

scenes.voiceover: Choose a process that is real, repeated, and has clear inputs and outputs. For example, supplier invoice intake, event registration, or customer enquiry triage.

scenes.on_screen_text: Decisions about people stay with people
scenes.voiceover: Avoid processes that make automated decisions about people. If yours touches hiring, credit, insurance or housing, the agent may only collect and summarise. A person decides, and your design must show that approval step.

slide.title: The one-page design
slide.body: 1 Trigger · 2 Steps (rule or model?) · 3 Tools (read or write?) · 4 Approval points and who approves · 5 Failure modes and responses · 6 Data: where it flows, sample data only

scenes.voiceover: Before you build, write a one-page design with six parts. The trigger that starts a run. The steps in order, marking which are rules and which use the model. The tools, and whether each one reads or writes. The approval points, and who approves. The failure modes, and what happens then. And the data: what flows where, and confirmation that it is sample data.

scenes.stock_query: architect sketching floor plan on paper
scenes.voiceover: Think of an architect's floor plan. You can move a wall on paper in a minute. Moving it after the concrete is poured takes weeks. Ten minutes on the design page saves hours of rebuilding nodes.

slide.title: Simplest version first
slide.body: Fixed workflow backbone → one AI step → agent only where steps depend on input. Checkpoint flag: runs end to end on 5 inputs.

scenes.voiceover: Then build the simplest version first. Start with a fixed workflow, and add an AI step where needed. Use the agent node only for the part where the steps really depend on the input. Get it running end to end on five inputs, before you add polish.

slide.title: Lan's design: the path
slide.body: Webhook (form submissions) → rule: reject empty → Claude: registration · session_change · dietary_request · refund_request · not_sure (validated JSON) → Switch → drafts to 'approvals'.

scenes.voiceover: Let's see an example. Nguyen Thi Lan organises conferences for an events company in Hanoi, Vietnam. She automates registration questions for a sample event. Her design starts with a webhook that receives form submissions. A rule rejects empty ones. Claude classifies each message, as validated data. A Switch routes it.

screen_steps: Open Lan's one-page design in a document editor
Scroll to Tools: get_registration (read), get_session_capacity (read), propose_session_change (writes a proposal only)
Scroll to Approval points: all replies; refund requests → finance staff
Scroll to Data: invented attendee names and emails only
scenes.voiceover: Session changes go to an agent with three tools. Two only read: registrations and session capacity. The third only writes a proposal row. Every reply needs approval, and every refund request goes to finance staff, never to the agent. And she uses only invented attendee names and emails.

screen_steps: Scroll to Failure modes in the design page
Highlight: invalid JSON → retry once, then review
Highlight: API down → retry, then error workflow
Highlight: session full → agent says so, proposes alternatives
scenes.voiceover: She also plans for failure. If the JSON is not valid, the workflow retries once, then sends the item to review. If the API is down, it retries, then the error workflow takes over. And if a session is full, the agent says so, and proposes alternatives.

screen_steps: Add a Webhook node and copy its test URL
Send one sample submission from a free API client
Add the IF rule rejecting empty submissions
Add the Claude HTTP Request with the classification prompt
Add the validation Code node from L06
scenes.voiceover: Now she builds. She adds a webhook node, copies its test address, and sends one sample submission from a free API client. Then she adds the rule, the Claude request, and the validation code from lesson six.

screen_steps: Add a Switch node on category
Connect session_change to an AI Agent with the Anthropic Chat Model
Attach the three tools: get_registration, get_session_capacity, propose_session_change
Connect every branch to Google Sheets append to 'approvals' with status = pending
scenes.voiceover: She adds a Switch, and connects session changes to an AI Agent, with the Anthropic chat model and her three tools. Every branch ends in the approvals tab, marked pending.

screen_steps: Send 5 test submissions, one per category
Open the executions list: 5 successful runs
Open the 'approvals' tab: 5 pending rows with drafts (example output)
scenes.voiceover: Finally, she sends five test submissions, one of each type. Each one lands in the approvals tab. In each row, you'll see something like a sensible draft. It works end to end. Error handling and the full test set come next.

scenes.on_screen_text: Mostly workflow. Agent only where needed.
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to design one agent that does everything, with ten tools and a long system message. It is hard to test, and hard to explain. Most of your process should be a clear workflow. Use the agent only where it is really needed, and keep write actions behind approval.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. A real, repeated process; people decide about people. 2. One-page design: trigger, steps, tools, approvals, failures, data. 3. Simplest version, end to end on 5 inputs.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, choose a real, repeated process, and keep a person in charge of any decision about people. Second, write a one-page design: trigger, steps, tools, approval points, failure modes and data. Third, build the simplest version that runs end to end on five inputs.

Now it is your turn. This is step one of your capstone. In the exercise below this video, you will write your design page, and build a working version of your agent that runs end to end on five test inputs, with Google Sheets and the Claude API. Allow about ninety minutes. In the next lesson, the final one, we cover Capstone: Test, Harden and Present. See you there.
